guideTitle: Best RV Water Heaters for Travel Trailers (2026)
metaTitle: Best RV Water Heaters for Travel Trailers
metaDescription: Five travel trailer water heaters compared on tank size, direct-fit swaps, tankless retrofits and the towing realities of weight, vibration and hookups.
expertTake: The Suburban SW12DE is the top pick for family travel trailers because twelve gallons of reserve, direct spark ignition and a 120V element suit weekend-to-week trips. The Suburban SAW6DE is the pick for owners swapping a failed 6 gallon aluminum heater without cutting anything. Skip tankless if you tow in freezing weather and cannot commit to a full drain.
introParagraphs: A travel trailer heater lives a rough life. It bounces down highways, sits for weeks in storage and then has to light on the first try at a campground. The best heater for that life is the one that survives vibration, thaws predictably and can be fixed by a dealer.

Most trailers come with a 6 or 10 gallon unit behind an exterior door, and most replacements are chosen by what already fits. What follows ranks five options that cover the common cases: direct-fit swaps, larger family tanks and two tankless retrofits for owners who want to reclaim space.

products.name: Suburban SW12DE 12-gallon DSI and electric heater
products.description:
The SW12DE is the large-family answer for a trailer that sees campgrounds more than back roads. Twelve gallons of porcelain-lined steel covers several short showers, the direct spark ignition does away with a standing pilot and the electric element means the heater works from a pedestal as well as from propane. In a typical towable it is the most forgiving pick for a household that does not want to schedule showers.

The tradeoff is weight and cabinet size. A full 12 gallon tank adds roughly 100 pounds of water, and the heater itself is large, so confirm that your cabinet and the tongue weight tolerate it. It also depends on 12V DC for ignition, which means a trailer battery that is dying will not light it, even when the cylinders are full.

Ownership is routine. Inspect the anode every spring, flush the tank with the drain plug out, check the burner tube for spiders and keep the bypass valves in the right position when you de-winterize. Many owners forget the bypass and conclude the heater is dead when the trailer is simply routing water around it. A second common spring miss is a drain plug left out or an anode rod fitting that was not resealed, which shows up as a puddle under the cabinet after the first fill.
products.bestFor: Family trailers that camp at hookups and want a big reserve.
pros: Twelve gallons covers a family's short showers
120V element helps at a campground pedestal
Direct spark ignition with no pilot to relight
Replaceable anode extends tank life
cons: Needs 12V DC to light the burner
Cabinet must accept a 12 gallon unit

products.name: Suburban SAW6DE 6-gallon direct-fit DSI heater
products.description:
The SAW6DE is built to replace six gallon aluminum tank heaters without modifying the cutout or the cabinet, which is the situation many owners find themselves in when an old tank rusts through or leaks. It has a porcelain-lined steel tank, a direct spark burner and an electric element, and it uses the existing door opening. That makes the swap a weekend job instead of a project.

The tradeoff is capacity. Six gallons is small for a family and the steel liner needs an anode that the old aluminum tank never did. Owners who forget that new maintenance item will see the tank age faster than they expect. Against the SW12DE you give up reserve, and against the aluminum models you take on a yearly chore.

It is a straightforward heater to keep alive. Pull the anode in spring, flush sediment, keep the burner tube clear and bypass the heater before antifreeze goes through the lines. If you tow in cold weather, plan to drain it completely rather than relying on the cabinet heat of a running furnace. The furnace warms the living space, not the exterior heater compartment, and a cold snap with a failed furnace can freeze a heater that you thought was protected.
products.bestFor: Replacing a failed 6 gallon aluminum tank heater without cutting the cabinet.
pros: Direct-fit design for 6 gallon aluminum openings
Electric element adds campground flexibility
Porcelain lining with a replaceable anode
Direct spark ignition
cons: Six gallons limits showers for a family

products.name: Suburban SW10DE 10-gallon DSI and electric heater
products.description:
The SW10DE splits the difference between the compact SAW6DE and the large SW12DE. Ten gallons is a comfortable size for a couple with a kid or two, and the porcelain-lined tank, replaceable anode and direct spark ignition match the larger model. The electric element is listed as optional, so check the suffix before you order.

The downside is that it is neither small nor large. If your cabinet takes a 12 gallon tank, you may as well have the extra reserve, and if your cabinet only fits a 6 gallon unit, the SW10DE will not drop in. It is the right choice for the owner whose existing opening is 10 gallon class and who wants a like-for-like swap.

Expect the standard Suburban routine: anode inspection, a sediment flush, a clear burner tube and a proper bypass for winter. Parts and service are common, which matters when a trailer fails on the road. Keep a spare anode, a drain plug and a spare fuse in the tow vehicle, since those three items solve most of the small failures that strand a weekend.
products.bestFor: Trailers with an existing 10 gallon cabinet that need a like-for-like heater.
pros: Ten gallons suits a small family
Direct spark ignition and electric option
Replaceable anode extends tank life
Common parts and widespread service
cons: Electric element is optional on some versions
Does not drop into a 6 gallon opening

products.name: FOGATTI InstaShower 8 Plus propane tankless heater
products.description:
FOGATTI's InstaShower 8 Plus offers three door sizes, which matters in a trailer fleet where the old tank heater may have been fitted by any of a dozen manufacturers. It is a propane tankless with 12V DC controls and a listed readiness to about 9,800 feet. A tankless frees the cabinet space a tank would use and can save some weight on the tongue.

The tradeoff is complexity and freezing. A trailer that sits in an unheated storage lot needs a careful drain, because even a small amount of water can crack an exchanger. It also needs steady flow and battery power, and a thin trailer battery with a corroded terminal will cause failed ignition more than the heater ever will.

Ownership is easier if you commit to a routine. Drain in autumn, flush in spring, check the exhaust and keep the propane regulator healthy. If your trailer's pump struggles at low flow, a tank may serve you better.
products.bestFor: Trailers with an odd cutout that want on-demand hot water.
pros: Three door sizes suit more cutouts
Frees cabinet space and trims weight
Listed ready for about 9,800 feet
Endless hot water while propane lasts
cons: Depends on steady flow and 12V power
No stored reserve if ignition fails

products.name: Hillhub 65,000 BTU propane tankless, 3.9 GPM
products.description:
The Hillhub lists 65,000 BTU, 3.9 GPM and CSA certification, and it is designed for a standard opening of about 12.8 by 12.8 inches. In a trailer it offers more raw output than the InstaShower 8 Plus, and the retrofit design aims at simple replacement. The three-second claim is a statement about the burner lighting, not about hot water reaching a far-away tap.

The tradeoff is the same as any tankless: freeze risk, flow dependence and power draw. It also uses a smaller opening than some trailers, so measure the cutout and compare it with the 12.8 inch figure. A mismatch means trimming and sealing.

Use it where you value burner headroom and short waits over reserve. Keep the exhaust clear, descale in hard water, drain fully for winter and replace the regulator when it ages. Since the Hillhub burner is large, a stable supply matters more than with a small tank, so a dual-stage regulator on the cylinders is a sensible upgrade for a trailer that already has one.
products.bestFor: Trailer owners who want maximum tankless output in a smaller opening.
pros: 65,000 BTU burner with a 3.9 GPM rating
CSA certification on the listing
Compact 12.8 inch retrofit design
Frees tank space and weight
cons: Smaller opening may not match every cutout
Freeze risk without a full drain

buyingCriteria.explanation: Most trailers have a 6 or 10 gallon cabinet sized to the original heater. The Suburban SAW6DE is described as a direct-fit swap for 6 gallon aluminum heaters, and the SW10DE and SW12DE match their own cabinets. A tankless like the Hillhub uses a 12.8 inch opening, so verify yours before ordering. A mismatched heater means carpentry, sealing and a weekend lost. Look at the old heater label for the model, the BTU rating and the gallon size, then compare those against the new listing line by line. If the label has worn away, measure the opening, the door and the flue spacing and send the measurements to the seller before you order.

A full 12 gallon tank holds roughly 100 pounds of water, and a 6 gallon unit about half that. Trailers are sensitive to tongue weight, so drain the heater before towing if you can. A tankless unit carries only a cup of water and saves weight in the cabinet. For a trailer near its tongue weight limit, that saving is worth real attention, because every pound at the front changes how the trailer sways at highway speed.

If you stay at pedestals, an electric element on the SW12DE, SW10DE or SAW6DE saves propane and speeds recovery. If you boondock, propane matters more. The element draws roughly 12 amps at 120V, which is a large share of a 30 amp pedestal, so avoid running it with an air conditioner. A simple habit is to heat water with the element before breakfast, then switch to propane while the air conditioner or microwave runs, so you stay under the breaker.

Heaters ride through potholes and washboard roads. Check that burner tubes, wiring and gas fittings stay tight after a long trip. A loose connector is the quiet cause of many no-light calls in the spring. Wiggle the 12V connectors at the heater, look for green corrosion on the terminals and confirm the ground strap is tight, because a bad ground behaves exactly like a dead igniter.

A trailer in an unheated lot sees freezing nights. A tank can be drained and bypassed, and a tankless must have its exchanger completely emptied. Never run antifreeze through the heater, and open the drain and relief valve before storing the trailer. If you tow in winter to a heated site, drain anyway, because a roadside stop in freezing weather can crack a heater before you get to a campground.

Suburban heaters are the most familiar to RV technicians, so a failure far from home is usually fixable quickly. Newer tankless brands may need shipped parts. Weigh that difference against the benefits you want. A tankless that saves cabinet space is not a bargain if a failed board strands you for two weeks, so a clear parts list and a responsive seller belong in your decision.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cabinet compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each listing describes fit, such as direct-fit for 6 gallon aluminum heaters on the SAW6DE. Heaters that avoid cabinet changes scored higher, because every cut, caulk joint and bracket adds a leak path and an hour of labor. We also noted when the listing named the old heater it replaces, which is a stronger fit statement than a general claim.

howWeEvaluated.title: Family capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 6, 10 and 12 gallon tanks against tankless output. A larger tank serves a family, while a tankless gives endless hot water at the cost of power and flow. We weighed the stored reserve of a tank against the space savings of a tankless, and we treated the family size as the deciding factor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Towing weight and vibration
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the weight of water and the mechanical simplicity of each design. Fewer moving parts and lighter service weight earned credit, and we asked how each design copes with a rough road, since a loose igniter lead or a shifting tank is a common source of problems.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hookup flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether the heater uses propane, electricity or both. Dual-fuel tanks served campground and boondocking users better, because they keep working when one source is missing. We also noted the amp draw of each element against a typical pedestal.

howWeEvaluated.title: Parts and dealer support
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed brand reach and service familiarity, since a trailer breakdown happens away from home. Suburban wide parts availability scored well, and so did listings that include a clear manual and part numbers. A heater that cannot be repaired locally has to be better in other ways to justify the risk.

rows: Six gallons and a direct-fit swap

cards.label: Direct fit
cards.text: The SAW6DE, SW10DE and SW12DE replace like with like. They are the fast, low-risk path when your cabinet is intact.

cards.label: Retrofit
cards.text: The InstaShower 8 Plus and Hillhub change the heater type and may need trimming or sealing. They suit owners who want to reclaim space.

howToChoose.note: Choose direct fit for a quick swap; choose a retrofit only if you accept the extra work. Many owners who start a tankless retrofit find the project is half done before they discover a bracket or a gas line that needs rerouting, so give yourself a full weekend and a dry day.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An electric element, a reserve large enough for a morning rush and simple service. Avoid stacking the element with air conditioning on a 30 amp pedestal.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Suburban SW12DE and SW10DE both include elements, and the SW12DE gives the largest reserve. Before you choose, check what else runs on the pedestal during a typical morning, because the element competes with the coffee maker, the converter and the air conditioner.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You tow often or live in the trailer. The SW12DE's reserve and Suburban's service network reduce downtime.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp a few weekends a year. The SAW6DE is enough.

maintenance.why: Steel tanks depend on it. Replace at about three quarters consumed.
Vibration loosens connections. A quick check prevents spring no-light calls.
Sediment lowers recovery. Drain through the plug and rinse.
Spider webs cause yellow flames and failed ignition. Brush the tube clear.
Water in a tank or exchanger can freeze. Never leave antifreeze in the heater.

faq.q: Which size suits a travel trailer?
faq.a: Six gallons suits a couple on weekend trips, ten a small family, and twelve a larger family. Match the existing cabinet first, because size follows the opening.

faq.q: Should I choose gas only or gas-electric?
faq.a: Gas-electric is better if you use hookups, because the element saves propane and shortens recovery. Gas-only is fine if you mostly boondock.

faq.q: Why is there no hot water after storage?
faq.a: The most common cause is a bypass valve left in the winterize position. Check it before assuming the heater is dead. After that, confirm the 12V supply, the propane valve and the burner tube, in that order, and you will solve most spring surprises without a service call.

Yes, a tankless holds almost no water, so the cabinet weight is lower. It still needs a careful winter drain, and a trailer stored outdoors benefits from a low-point drain that you can open in seconds.

faq.q: Is the electric element safe with an air conditioner?
faq.a: A 1440W element draws about 12 amps. On a 30 amp pedestal, running it with an air conditioner can trip the breaker.

faq.q: Can I swap an aluminum heater for a steel one?
faq.a: Yes, a direct-fit unit like the SAW6DE is designed for that, but it adds an anode rod to your maintenance list.
